180.bp: Scientists spend huge amounts of time hunting through papers to support claims they've written. The real goal is to ground author statements in actual published work, catching both honest mistakes and catching yourself before you cite something that doesn't actually say what you think it says.
180.wh: Language models are great at writing but terrible at inventing facts (they make up citations). At the same time, researchers don't want their private papers sent to distant servers during the writing process — and if the system just asks an LLM to find citations, you get hallucinated paper titles and author names that sound plausible but don't exist.
180.ap: CiteLLM lives inside your LaTeX editor and never sends your writing to the cloud. It uses the LLM only to turn your claim into a good search query and to rank and explain results. The actual citations it retrieves come directly from trusted databases like academic repositories, not from the LLM's memory.
180.ww: By separating jobs — letting the LLM only do what it's good at (rephrasing your idea into search terms and explaining why a paper matches) while forcing actual results to come from a real database — you get the efficiency of AI without the fabrication. The LLM can't hallucinate a paper that isn't in the index.
180.po: You get valid, usable citations without privacy leaks and without made-up references. In their evaluation, the system returned significantly more correct citations than alternatives, and researchers could trust every result.

181.bp: Image classifiers trained on web photos learn to recognize objects, but web data is messy and biased. In reality, pictures of 'doctor' are mostly white men, pictures of 'nurse' are mostly women, and classifiers absorb these biases wholesale. When that classifier is deployed in hiring or content moderation, it perpetuates social unfairness.
181.wh: The obvious fix—just get more balanced data—is expensive and slow. The real tension is that in the training set, images with bias (e.g., women as nurses) vastly outnumber images without the bias (e.g., men as nurses), so the network confidently learns the spurious correlation. Standard balancing tricks require manual labels or synthetic data.
181.ap: BiasEdit first finds hidden biases by comparing visual and text representations to spot which attributes (like gender) are unfairly linked to classes. Then it uses off-the-shelf image editing tools to rewrite those attributes in biased images—turning a photo of a male nurse into one that preserves his role but removes the gender signal—creating synthetic balanced data automatically.
181.ww: Editing images at the visual level preserves realism better than mixing pixels, and by using existing text-image understanding models, you don't need a separate expensive bias detector. The network then trains on balanced data without bias-conflict examples being rare or artificial-looking.
181.po: Classifiers trained on the edited dataset stop picking up gender and other social attributes as cues for classification, reducing unfairness significantly without manual annotation and without requiring retraining from scratch.

182.bp: Kubernetes clusters break in complex ways, and when they do, teams need to diagnose the problem fast. The real-world goal is to use past resolutions to speed up future diagnosis—learn from what happened last time a node crashed or a pod hung.
182.wh: Most AI diagnosis systems have fixed knowledge (they know about 50 common Kubernetes errors) but never improve from new cases they encounter. Language models are huge, so deploying them requires either sending logs to a cloud vendor or licensing an expensive service, both risky in production.
182.ap: MetaKube is a smaller 8-billion-parameter model (KubeLLM) trained specifically on 7,000 real Kubernetes incidents. It stores past resolutions in a memory system that remembers which patterns led to solutions, and a reasoning controller decides whether to take the fast path (pattern recognition) or the deep path (detailed analysis) based on how familiar the problem is.
182.ww: Because the model is trained only on Kubernetes data and stays on your own servers, it's both faster and more accurate than generic LLMs. The memory system lets it recognize recurring problems instantly, and the reasoning layer makes sure it doesn't skip analysis on novel issues.
182.po: The system diagnoses Kubernetes problems correctly 90% of the time (up from 51% with the untrained baseline), runs entirely locally with no data leaving your cluster, and continues to improve as it encounters and remembers new faults.

183.bp: Online ads cost money, and advertisers need to decide how much to spend on each campaign to win valuable user interactions within a fixed budget. The real goal is to maximize the value of ad impressions won, when each advertiser has different goals and little historical data to learn from.
183.wh: Advertisers often know their objectives but have very few past interactions to learn from (few-shot problem). Standard reinforcement learning needs lots of trial and error to find good bidding strategies, and it can't generalize from one advertiser's patterns to another's.
183.ap: DARA splits the job into two stages. First, an LLM reads the advertiser's situation (budget, history, goals) and reasons through an initial plan in plain language. Second, a fine-tuned optimizer takes that plan and refines it numerically using feedback, learning exactly how much more value each dollar spent earns.
183.ww: LLMs are good at reasoning from a few examples (they've seen billions of text descriptions of decision-making), so they can draft a reasonable strategy quickly. But they're imprecise at math, so the second stage fixes the numbers. This split lets you leverage LLM generalization without accuracy loss.
183.po: On real advertising data, DARA consistently outbids traditional reinforcement learning approaches, even when history is sparse, and adapts quickly to new advertiser profiles without retraining.

184.bp: People can now generate realistic fake images of faces on their phones, creating serious privacy and forgery risks. Researchers have built invisible digital protections that scramble photos so AI face generators can't use them, but attackers keep finding ways around those protections.
184.wh: Privacy protections work by adding subtle noise to images so generated fakes lose quality and don't look like the real person. But face restoration algorithms—tools designed to clean up blurry or damaged photos—can undo that noise and recover the original appearance, defeating the protection.
184.ap: The paper proves mathematically why face restoration is so effective at breaking privacy protections: it's specifically designed to recover detail from degraded images, which is exactly what privacy noise looks like to the restoration algorithm. They also show that fine-tuning the restoration model makes attacks even more effective.
184.ww: Face restoration works because it models what real faces look like and uses that model to invent missing details. Privacy noise looks like missing detail, so the restoration algorithm competes with the privacy protection in a race to define what details get added back.
184.po: The paper demonstrates that state-of-the-art privacy protections for images are vulnerable to this simple attack, significantly stronger than prior red-teaming methods, and calls out the urgent need for better protections against this specific threat.

185.bp: On social media, people often say sarcastic things to mock, criticize, or make jokes. To understand online content fairly, AI needs to both detect sarcasm is happening and explain what the person really meant—the detection and the explanation are two sides of the same understanding.
185.wh: Text, images, and video all contribute to sarcasm, but they contribute in different ways. Most systems treat detection and explanation as separate problems, missing that a good explanation should logically support why something is sarcastic. Also, multimodal sarcasm requires combining text and visual cues, but simply averaging representations from text and images loses important context.
185.ap: MuVaC models the reasoning process as a causal chain: the detection ("this is sarcasm") should be explained by a reason extracted from the multimodal content. It uses a statistical causal framework to ensure detection and explanation are consistent with each other. A specialized fusion method combines text and image features in a way that preserves both what each modality contributes.
185.ww: By enforcing that detection and explanation must be causally aligned, the model can't claim something is sarcastic without pointing to what makes it sarcastic. This mirrors how humans actually understand sarcasm—we both recognize it and know why we think so, as a single act of reasoning.
185.po: On test datasets, MuVaC detects sarcasm more accurately and generates more trustworthy explanations than systems that treat detection and explanation separately, and the explanations align better with why the detection happened.

186.bp: AI agents now generate text, images, and code at scale on the web. When one agent consumes content another agent created, both need to know where it came from, what settings were used, and whether it can be legally reused—otherwise errors propagate and licenses get violated.
186.wh: AI-generated content has no inherent metadata. You can't tell if a piece of text was written by an LLM, what prompt was used, what model version created it, or whether it's licensed for reuse. This is especially dangerous when agents feed each other content and errors accumulate (one wrong fact gets refined into five more wrong facts).
186.ap: This framework wraps generated content with structured metadata at creation time: the prompt used, model name, hyperparameters, confidence scores, and context. This metadata is packaged with verifiable credentials (cryptographic proof that it wasn't tampered with) so downstream agents can trust it.
186.ww: Metadata attached at the moment of creation is trustworthy because you can cryptographically verify it hasn't been altered. Agents can then check whether they're allowed to reuse content (license check), whether the creation settings are appropriate for their task, and trace errors back to their source.
186.po: Downstream applications like model fine-tuning and knowledge distillation can now safely consume AI-generated content because they know its provenance and can verify it meets legal and technical requirements.

187.bp: Recommendation systems, fraud detection, and knowledge bases all rely on graphs of connections between users, items, and concepts. In the real world, these graphs are constantly changing, get attacked by adversaries, and contain missing or outdated information—and the AI systems trained on them fail silently.
187.wh: Most research assumes the graph is clean and stable. In reality, web data is messy: a bot injects fake follows to game recommendations, a server goes down and loses data, or the patterns users follow today are totally different from yesterday. Algorithms trained on yesterday's graph become unreliable.
187.ap: This tutorial surveys defenses at multiple levels: cleaning data before it enters the system (preprocessing), making the model itself more resistant to corruption (model-level adaptation), and ensuring the model can generalize when the world changes (generalization techniques).
187.ww: Robustness requires thinking about where failures come from. Some are data problems (bad inputs), some are model problems (overfitting to unstable patterns), and some are environmental (domain shift). Addressing all three angles gives more resilience than trying to solve them all at once.
187.po: The tutorial provides researchers and engineers with a structured way to think about robustness in graph systems, concrete methods to apply, and real-world examples showing how these defenses help in recommender systems and fraud detection.

188.bp: Big hospitals, drug companies, and engineering firms want AI to learn from human expert feedback to improve models, but experts can't share raw case data due to privacy laws and intellectual property protection. The goal is to collect feedback safely without seeing the sensitive data.
188.wh: Decentralized feedback collection lets experts keep their data private, but then you can't verify the feedback is correct. A lazy annotator might give wrong labels, or a malicious one might poison the data deliberately, and you'd never know.
188.ap: Trustless Feedback uses zero-knowledge proofs—cryptographic math that proves a fact is true without revealing the secret information behind it. The expert's case data stays on their machine. A proof certifies that their feedback satisfies hard constraints (e.g., "this drug combination has no interactions") without exposing the case details.
188.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs turn verification into a math problem. You don't need to see the data to verify it's valid, just like you don't need to see someone's birth certificate to verify they're over 18 if they show you a signed proof. This splits privacy from integrity checking.
188.po: Models trained on this feedback are guaranteed to reject invalid data (100% in their prototype) while never seeing the underlying sensitive cases, making it practical for hospitals and engineering firms to contribute expert feedback.

189.bp: Scientists publish research, but turning that raw text into a structured database of facts and contributions (a knowledge graph) is still mostly manual. The goal is to automatically extract machine-readable facts that other AI systems can use to verify claims and find related work.
189.wh: Language models can extract facts from text, but they're inconsistent. They might call the same concept 'deep learning' in one paper and 'neural networks' in another, making the resulting database messy and hard for downstream systems to use. Manual crowdsourcing is consistent but tedious and error-prone.
189.ap: LOPE uses an LLM to extract properties and concepts from papers, then aligns those extracted terms to a standardized vocabulary (an ontology). This normalization step turns 'deep learning' and 'neural networks' into the same canonical term, making the database consistent and machine-actionable.
189.ww: Extracting from text and then normalizing separately is more efficient than trying to extract into perfect terminology in one pass (which the LLM struggles with). The ontology acts as a translator, and using a well-designed vocabulary ensures downstream systems understand the data the same way.
189.po: The resulting scientific knowledge graph is semantically consistent—key facts are represented the same way across papers—and verified to be more consistent than manual crowdsourcing, making it useful for retrieval-augmented generation and hallucination detection in AI systems.

190.bp: Companies maintain separate knowledge bases for different business domains (one for products, one for customers, one for suppliers). When information is missing from one database, they want to infer it by borrowing patterns from the others—without the databases looking identical.
190.wh: If you try to share information across databases too directly, you lose important context specific to each domain. A 'supplier relationship' means something different in manufacturing versus retail, and forcing them to look the same washes out that specificity. Also, low-resource domains need help but shouldn't get overwritten by high-resource ones.
190.ap: DMKGC treats each database as a partial view of the full truth. It generates new entity representations using diffusion models (a technique that starts with noise and gradually denoises toward a target). The diffusion process is guided by matching entities across databases, but targets a domain-neutral representation to avoid bias.
190.ww: Diffusion models naturally balance constraints: they're pushed toward the guidance (shared entity information) but also pulled toward a neutral target (the prior representation). This prevents any single domain from dominating. The unbiased target ensures that adding support from other databases improves accuracy without distorting domain-specific knowledge.
190.po: Knowledge graphs trained this way complete missing triples (predict unknown relationships) more accurately than methods that enforce strict consistency, especially when some domains have very little training data.

191.bp: Modern cities generate vast data about where people go, how they move, and what patterns repeat over time. The goal is to understand human mobility and urban dynamics—both for planning (where to build transit) and analysis (detecting anomalies or predicting congestion).
191.wh: Spatio-temporal data is complex: a subway commute has structure (happens every weekday morning) but with variation (delays, weather, special events). Traditional statistical methods and even deep learning models struggle to generalize across different cities or adapt when patterns shift. Language models have seen descriptions of thousands of cities and mobility patterns in their training data.
191.ap: This tutorial covers how to apply large language models and foundation models to spatio-temporal analysis at three levels: finding patterns within a location (what happens at this intersection), understanding movement trajectories (how an individual commutes), and modeling regional flows (how traffic moves between neighborhoods).
191.ww: Language models are powerful at reasoning about spatial and temporal concepts because they've encountered descriptions in text. They can generate predictions in natural language or structured form, adapt quickly when you prompt them with new context, and transfer learning from one city to another better than models trained from scratch.
191.po: The tutorial maps out methods for LLM-based applications to urban computing, location-based services, and transportation systems, helping researchers think about which problems benefit from this new approach versus traditional deep learning.

192.bp: Language models connected to knowledge databases can answer hard questions by retrieving relevant facts first, then reasoning over them. The goal is to get accurate, explainable answers in domains like medicine where confidence matters—you need to know when to trust the model.
192.wh: Knowledge-augmented models are often overconfident. They might retrieve an incomplete sub-graph (missing key relationships) or unreliable information, but still predict with high confidence. In a hospital, an overconfident wrong answer is dangerous.
192.ap: Ca2KG uses counterfactual prompting: asking the model to imagine scenarios where certain retrieved facts are missing or changed, exposing whether it's really dependent on reliable information or just memorized patterns. Then it recalibrates confidence scores by averaging predictions across these hypothetical scenarios.
192.ww: Counterfactual reasoning exposes weaknesses in reasoning. If the model's answer changes dramatically when you remove one retrieved fact, then it was over-relying on that fact. By re-scoring based on robustness across interventions, you get confidence levels that actually reflect uncertainty.
192.po: On question-answering benchmarks, Ca2KG produces calibrated confidence scores (it's more uncertain when it should be) while maintaining or improving accuracy, making it safer for high-stakes applications.

193.bp: Large language models run on phones and edge devices because of quantization—a compression technique that makes models smaller and faster. But this compression happens at a layer where attackers can inject hidden behaviors, like making the model refuse to answer normal questions or bypass safety filters.
193.wh: Quantization reduces precision of model weights to save space, but defending it is hard. You have very limited data to work with (just a small calibration set), each layer gets compressed independently (restricting global attacks), and you can't use gradients to guide an attack (quantization is a fixed operation).
193.ap: LLMQuA injects backdoors by editing only the quantized weights directly, without needing gradients. It uses data-efficient knowledge editing (changing the model's behavior with just a few token pairs) and adjusts quantization parameters layer-by-layer to maintain the original activation patterns while hiding malicious changes.
193.ww: By working directly on quantized weights and using knowledge editing instead of gradient-based poisoning, the attack bypasses all three defenses. The model appears normal on general tasks but misbehaves on specific triggers, like refusing to engage with content moderation rules.
193.po: The paper demonstrates that quantized language models, when deployed locally, are vulnerable to this attack: 68% of moderation cases can be evaded and 90% of targeted queries get refused, while the model's normal utility only drops slightly.

194.bp: Information spreads through social networks—memes, news, behaviors ripple outward as people share and adopt. To predict what will happen next, platforms and researchers model who will adopt based on the history of how others already have.
194.wh: Most models treat adoption as a sequence of individuals choosing independently, computing influence one-to-one (person A influences person B). But that's slow—for a cascade of 10,000 people, you'd need billions of pairwise calculations. Also, real influence is often collective (a group trend makes adoption likely), not individual.
194.ap: GRID groups users and models influence between groups instead of between individuals. It learns group identities by maximizing information about key influence pathways while discarding noise (information bottleneck principle), then uses a specialized attention module that computes group-to-group influence in linear time instead of quadratic.
194.ww: Grouping reduces complexity dramatically: instead of checking if person 10,000 influences person 10,001, you check if their groups interact. This scales to ultra-long cascades. Also, groups better represent real influence: a trend spreading through 50 tech workers is more real than 50 independent binary decisions.
194.po: GRID models information cascades with over 10,000 users without truncating history (prior work could only handle hundreds), maintains accuracy within a mathematically-proven error bound, and dramatically reduces computation, making prediction on large social networks practical.
